entities.summary:
The First Macedonian War was a pivotal conflict between ancient Rome and the kingdom of Macedon, fought between 214 and 205 BCE, and led by the Roman consul T. Quinctius Flamininus and the Macedonian king Philip V. This war marked a turning point in the Hellenistic period, as Rome emerged as a dominant power in the Mediterranean.

The war began in 214 BCE, when Philip V of Macedon formed an alliance with Hannibal, the Carthaginian general, in an attempt to counter the growing Roman influence in the region. The Roman consul T. Quinctius Flamininus, however, was able to rally support from the other Greek city-states and launch a successful campaign against the Macedonians. The war ended in 205 BCE, with Rome victorious and Macedon reduced to a Roman protectorate.

The legacy of the First Macedonian War can be seen in the subsequent rise of Rome as a major power in the Mediterranean. The war marked the beginning of Rome's expansion into the Greek world, which would continue for centuries. The war also had a profound impact on the development of the Roman Republic, as it led to the establishment of a more centralized and efficient government. As the Roman statesman and historian Polybius noted, 'the war between Rome and Macedon was a turning point in the history of the world'

The First Macedonian War also had a lasting impact on the geography of the Mediterranean, as it led to the establishment of Roman control over key regions and cities. The war also saw the rise of the Roman general Aemilius Paulus, who would go on to play a key role in future Roman campaigns. Ultimately, the First Macedonian War was a defining moment in the ancient world, as it marked the beginning of Rome's dominance over the Mediterranean and set the stage for centuries of Roman expansion.
